title: Is Cristiano Ronaldo still not done? Is Spain the World Cup’s most complete team? Day 22 recap
content:
Get free access to the most comprehensive World Cup coverage in The Athletic app

Spain, finally, looked again like the team that won the Euros two years ago. It made quite the statement in its 3-0 win against Austria and left the impression that this World Cup isn’t necessarily going to be a procession for France. “Today’s performance should be the foundation for what comes next,” Luis de la Fuente said. And up next in Dallas on July 6 is Portugal who managed to see off Croatia in a wild game in Toronto.

Belatedly, Ronaldo scored his first goal in a World Cup knockout stage only to be, courageously, replaced late in the game by Roberto Martinez. Unexpectedly, Goncalo Ramos ended up the hero with a winner against the run of play to keep Portugal in the competition. His header likely brought the curtain down on Luka Modric’s World Cup career. The Milan midfielder, a prospective future teammate of Ramos, won the Ballon d’Or after leading Croatia to the final in 2018. He then helped this nation, with its population of under 4 million, return to the semis four years later in Qatar.

“Well, this was probably his last World Cup,” Croatia coach Zlatko Dalic said. “And I’m sorry it ended this way. Very sadly, with a defeat. Luka played in the second half and was again one of our key players. I feel really sorry that it ended this way. He has shown his quality and his character and he was leading Croatia to the end.”

Switzerland was the third European nation to progress from Thursday’s games, defeating Algeria 2-0 in Vancouver with early goals in each half from Breel Embolo and Dan Ndoye. The Swiss will stay in Vancouver and take on either Colombia or Ghana on July 7.

Matchday 22 results

Spain 3-0 Austria
Portugal 2-1 Croatia
Switzerland 2-0 Algeria

Four years ago in Qatar, Goncalo Ramos offered a glimpse of what Portugal’s future might look like without Cristiano Ronaldo. The then-Benfica striker took his place against Switzerland and seized his opportunity. He scored a hat-trick in a 6-1 win and, just like that, rather prematurely, Ronaldo’s World Cup career was declared over. In Toronto on Thursday night, he was still leading the line, showing why it isn’t. At least, for now.

Portugal’s round-of-32 game against wily Croatia was one of Ronaldo’s best-ever performances at a World Cup. It is, strangely for him and his high standards, quite a low bar. Ronaldo justified his selection by scoring his first knockout goal, an equaliser, in this, his sixth World Cup. It came from the penalty spot rather than open play, although Ronaldo had earlier seen a goal disallowed for the narrowest of offsides. It was a pity, as the 41-year-old had deftly brought the ball down and then lifted it over the goalkeeper.

Having played every single minute at the World Cup, Ronaldo would have expected to stay on until the end. Portugal needed a goal and whenever it has needed one over the last two decades, it has nearly always looked to him. So it came as a something of a shock when coach Martinez substituted him for Ruben Neves in the 81st minute. Ronaldo looked briefly confused but Martinez’s changes, which started with an earlier quadruple substitution, including the withdrawal of Vitinha, were courageous.

“When you need a late goal, you can call Goncalo Ramos,” said, er, Ramos. The new Milan club-record signing headed in a delightfully whipped Rafa Leao cross, a sign, perhaps, of things to come under Ruben Amorim at San Siro next season. Ramos knows better than to think he has taken Ronaldo’s place in this Portugal team. But these surely are Ronaldo’s last games at a World Cup.

Past experiences must have flashed before his eyes at the end. Croatia had one goal disallowed after another, first from Petar Sucic then Josko Gvardiol. When the last one made Diogo Costa’s net billow deep into stoppage time, Ronaldo must have feared the worst. No one wants to go to extra time and penalties with Croatia. An on-field review prevented that outcome and a relieved Ronaldo, powerless to affect events on the sideline, celebrated the news.

It was, overall, a night of mixed emotions for him. He was happy to score. Surprised to come off. Delighted to go through. Emotional about Diogo Jota. His eyes welled up, as he pulled on Jota’s old 21 jersey, took it off and held it up for a team photo. Today is the anniversary of Jota’s death and that of his brother, Andre Silva, in a car accident. “We knew it before the game. It was a so special moment,” Ronaldo told FOX. “We speak today, our group, about that. The coincidence of life. I was amazed because the situation of today, it means a lot to us.”

After the US eliminated Bosnia in Santa Clara, the atmosphere behind the Fox stage was wild. Landon Donovan turned to Carli Lloyd and understandably got carried away. He echoed Mauricio Pochettino’s line: “Why not us?” Having confessed to being “so stressed in the last 15 minutes, that even my fake hair was falling off”, Donovan swiftly changed his tone. He didn’t see why the U.S. couldn’t go all the way. Here’s one reason why: Spain. If the U.S. overcomes an underwhelming Belgium in Seattle and Spain gets revenge on Portugal for its defeat in last summer’s Nations League final, the quarter-final between them in LA on July 10 should undoubtedly be the biggest test of the “Why not us?” mantra.

Spain put in, arguably, the most complete performance of the tournament against Austria on Thursday. Better as a whole, perhaps, than some of the combinations from France’s irresistible attack. La Roja didn’t allow a single shot on target and had 65 per cent possession in its comprehensive 3-0 win at SoFi. Mikel Oyarzabal may not have the profile of the tournament’s other leading strikers. He has remained in San Sebastian with Real Sociedad even after scoring Spain’s 86th-minute winner in the 2024 European Championship final against England. Don’t sleep on him.

The win meant coach Luis de la Fuente is still unbeaten in major tournament knockout games and seemed to indicate Spain are growing into this tournament.  More than the US, they look the most likely team to be able to stop France if both reach the semi-finals. Speaking to The Athletic, Pablo Zabaleta, now a member of the FIFA Study Group, said: “The best way to defend against France is by having possession and not letting France be on the ball. Only a few teams can do this. They could be Spain. They could be Argentina. Teams that can keep long possessions against them.”

Spain, you may recall, followed winning the Euros in 2008 by lifting the World Cup in 2010. Oyarzabal’s goal, incidentally and quite incredibly, was Spain’s first in the knockouts of this tournament since Andres Iniesta’s euphoric shirtless tribute to Dani Jarque in the final against the Netherlands in Johannesburg. Is history about to repeat itself?

One of the revelations of the World Cup has undoubtedly been Johan Manzambi.

A midfielder who wears the No 9, he plays out wide for Switzerland because Granit Xhaka and Remo Freuler are guarantees at the heart of the team. Initially used as a sub by Murat Yakin, the 20-year-old’s impact has been so great when coming on that his coach came under pressure to find a way to get him into the starting XI. Manzambi scored twice against Bosnia, including an over-the-shoulder volley, and got the winner against co-hosts Canada.

On Thursday, he drove into the Algeria penalty box, left a defender in his wake and then pulled the ball back for Breel Embolo’s tap-in. A member of the Freiburg team that reached the Conference League final, his versatility was on display against Crystal Palace too, where he played as a more advanced midfielder than usual as cover for the injured Yuito Suzuki.

Manzambi did not need a good World Cup to whip up interest from a host of Premier League clubs. He already had it and Freiburg must now sense an auction. Together with Morocco’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, he is one of the most coveted young players at the tournament.

Lionel Messi is playing at home. For the first time in the World Cup, he returns to Miami for Argentina’s round-of-32 clash against Cape Verde, the revelation of the tournament so far.

Few people are anticipating a shock but as Lionel Scaloni warned in his pre-match press conference, Argentina can’t be too casual. Memories of the opening-game defeat to Saudi Arabia four years ago linger, even though Argentina went on to win the World Cup, retain the Copa America and defeat Italy in the Finalissima.

It is also Scaloni’s 100th game in charge of the Albiceleste. No one — not Carlos Bilardo, nor Cesar Luis Menotti — has been as successful at the helm of the national team. While much of the success is attributed to Messi, credit is due to Scaloni for finding a way to make the eight-time Ballon d’Or winner express himself as well for his country as he does for his clubs.

Elsewhere, Egypt is sweating on Mohamed Salah’s fitness in Kansas City. Salah needed substituting in Egypt’s final group-stage game, a 1-1 draw against Iran, because of a hamstring strain. The 34-year-old, who left Liverpool at the end of last season, is in the squad to play Australia but it’s unclear whether or not he’ll start.

Closing out the day, Colombia takes on Ghana in Dallas. Nestor Lorenzo’s team has quietly impressed so far and should have won all of its group games. It only drew 0-0 with Portugal because Davinson Sanchez had a goal disallowed for the smallest infraction. His big toe was offside. “Next time I’ll ask him to get a pedicure,” Lorenzo laughed.

Ghana will be a tough nut to crack. If the Black Stars defends as resolutely against Colombia as it did against England, it could be a late one and follow Germany-Paraguay and Netherlands-Morocco in going to penalties.
